introduction.text:
Monte Testaccio is an artificial mound in Rome, located just east of the Tiber near the Horrea Galbae.  The hill rises to about 35 m and covers roughly 2 ha, making it one of the largest spoil heaps in the ancient world.

It is composed almost entirely of broken amphorae—over 53 million fragments, most of which were olive‑oil vessels from the Spanish region of Baetica.  The sheer volume of oil, estimated at 6 billion litres, reflects the scale of Rome’s state‑sponsored olive‑oil trade.

Excavations show that the mound was built in a deliberate, terraced fashion, with retaining walls of intact amphorae and lime sprinkled over the sherds to neutralise odours.  The organisation suggests a state administrative authority overseeing the disposal.

After the dumping ceased in the late 3rd century, the hill became a popular recreational site in the 19th century, hosting festivals, jousts, and the October gatherings described by Stendhal.  During the 1849 siege of Rome, Giuseppe Garibaldi commanded a gun battery on its summit, and the hill was also used as a symbolic representation of Golgotha on Good Friday, a tradition that still leaves a cross on the peak.

The first archaeological investigation was led by the German archaeologist Heinrich Dressel in 1872, whose work laid the foundation for later studies.

history.description: Monte Testaccio was built as a structured waste dump for broken olive‑oil amphorae, with deposits dated from roughly 140 AD to 250 AD, reflecting the peak of Rome’s olive‑oil imports.
The dumping of amphorae ceased around the 260s, possibly due to the relocation of the city’s quays and the introduction of a new amphora type.
In the 19th century the hill became a popular recreational spot, hosting festivals, jousts, and the annual October gatherings described by Stendhal and other travelers.
On Good Friday the hill was symbolically turned into a representation of Golgotha, with a cross placed on the summit that remains to this day.
During the 1849 siege of Rome, the summit was used as a gun battery commanded by Giuseppe Garibaldi, illustrating its strategic value.

design.description: The mound consists of several terraces built with retaining walls of intact amphorae filled with sherds, and lime was sprinkled over the broken pots to neutralise odours, indicating a highly organised construction process.
